blocks.text: The disagreement includes eating or abstaining, drinking wine, and assigning special value to certain days. Romans does not provide enough information to identify each side completely, so equating the “weak” simply with Jews or the “strong” simply with gentiles goes beyond the passage. Nor does the chapter establish universal vegetarianism or a required calendar. Its opening command is to welcome the person without turning that welcome into a hearing designed to settle every disputed opinion.

Paul holds together his conviction that nothing is unclean in itself and the reality that a person who regards something as unclean must not be pressured to violate that conviction. Eating, abstaining, and observing days are placed within personal assurance, action directed to the Lord, and thanksgiving. Unity therefore does not require identical diets or calendars. At the same time, conscience is not permission to control everyone else: those with greater freedom are told to restrain practices that grieve or destroy another.

Acts and Paul’s letters should not be collapsed into a single undifferentiated account of food disputes. Acts narrates an earlier council from a later compositional horizon, while Romans is an occasional letter addressing its own circumstances. This cautions against allowing Acts 15 to replace Paul’s argument here, just as Paul’s silence about that decree should not be used to erase the account in Acts.
